title: Trauma & the Freeze Response
hook: When escape seems impossible, bodies sometimes stop moving altogether, and the stillness that follows is not calm, consent or indifference.
why:
Most people know the phrase *fight or flight*. Fewer know that bodies have other answers to danger, and that one of the most common is to stop moving. People freeze in assaults, accidents, attacks and disasters, often to their own lasting shame, because they believe they should have fought or run. Afterwards, many carry their bodies differently for months or years: jumping at noises, scanning rooms, sitting with their backs to the wall, going suddenly still when something reminds them of what happened.

This chapter teaches you to recognise those responses and to respond in ways that help rather than harm. You will learn the full range of the body's defences, why freezing is not a choice, what life looks like when the body's alarm stays on, how reminders can pull the past into the present, the habits that make you safer company for someone who has been through trauma, why you should never make anyone tell their story, and the encouraging fact that treatment works. Nothing here is a way to diagnose anyone. It is a way to be a safe person to be near.

teach.h: Bodies have more than two answers to danger.
teach.p:
In 2015 Kasia Kozlowska and colleagues reviewed what is known about the body's defence responses across animals and humans, and described them as a cascade. When a threat appears, the first response is arousal: the body becomes alert and orients towards the danger. If action seems possible, the next is fight or flight. Freezing, in this account, is a state of alert stillness in which fight or flight is put on hold: the body is primed to move but holds still, perhaps to avoid being noticed, while it assesses what to do.

If escape seems impossible and the threat is overwhelming, the cascade can go further. Tonic immobility is a last-resort state in which the body becomes unable to move or speak, sometimes rigid, while the person remains aware of what is happening. Collapsed immobility goes further still: muscle tone is lost and the person may faint or become barely conscious. Kozlowska and colleagues describe these later responses as involuntary, driven by ancient brain systems rather than by any decision.

For a reader, the cascade explains behaviour that otherwise seems baffling. A man who went completely still when he was attacked, a woman who could not scream, a child who went limp, a soldier who froze under fire: none of them chose it, and none of them failed. Their bodies did what bodies do when the threat seems too great for fighting or running.

It also explains why stillness in the face of threat can be so easily misread, by observers, by courts, and by the people themselves.

Fight and flight are not the only options the body has. Sometimes the body chooses stillness, and the person is not consulted.
teach.disconfirm: If people facing overwhelming threat always fought or fled, with freezing and immobility rare, the cascade would describe animals more than humans. The research on human responses to assault and disaster, including the study described next, found immobility to be common.
teach.pullQuote: Sometimes the body chooses stillness, and the person is not consulted.

teach.p:
In 2017 Anna Möller, Hans Peter Söndergaard and Lotti Helström studied women who came to an emergency clinic in Stockholm after a sexual assault. They asked about tonic immobility during the assault: whether the women had felt unable to move or cry out despite wanting to. Of nearly three hundred women, around seven in ten reported significant immobility, and almost half reported extreme immobility. Those who had experienced it were more likely to develop post-traumatic stress and severe depression in the months afterwards.

The study involved women, but the same response occurs in men during assaults, robberies and other violence. Many male survivors describe the same shame: *why didn't I do anything?*

The findings matter for three reasons. First, they show that freezing during an assault is common, not unusual. Second, they show that it is involuntary, which means that a person who froze did not consent, did not cooperate and did not fail. The chapter on touch made the same point: stillness is not a yes. Third, they show that freezing is linked to later distress, partly because survivors so often blame themselves for it.

For a reader, the practical consequence is simple and important. Never ask someone who has been assaulted why they did not fight back, and never read their stillness at the time as agreement. If they blame themselves for freezing, you can tell them, truthfully, that freezing is one of the body's most common responses to overwhelming danger, and that it is not a choice.

Stillness under threat is a defence, not a decision.
teach.disconfirm: If people who froze during assaults turned out, when asked carefully, to have been able to move and to have chosen not to, the involuntary account would be wrong. The research on tonic immobility, and survivors' own accounts, describe the opposite.

teach.h: After trauma, the alarm can stay on.
teach.p:
After a frightening event, most people are shaken for a while: sleep is broken, the event replays in their mind, they feel on edge. For many, this settles over weeks. For some, it does not, and the body behaves as though the danger is still present.

The signs are often visible to the people around them. Hypervigilance: scanning rooms on entering, checking exits, sitting with the back to a wall, watching the door. An exaggerated startle: a dropped pan or a slammed door produces a jump, a flinch or a sudden stillness out of all proportion. Irritability and a short fuse. Poor sleep and nightmares. Avoidance of places, people or activities connected to what happened: the high street where the attack took place, driving after a crash, crowds after a terror attack. Some people seem numb or far away, as if part of them has switched off.

When these persist for more than about a month and disrupt life, clinicians may assess for post-traumatic stress disorder. That assessment belongs to a doctor or psychologist, not to you. But the signs are worth recognising, because they are often misread: the jumpy man as nervous, the irritable man as bad-tempered, the man who will not go into town as stubborn.

It helps to understand these behaviours as the body's learned protection. After a threat, the alarm system has been retuned to fire earlier and louder. That is exhausting to live with, and it is not weakness.

An alarm that keeps ringing is not a fault in the person. It is a body still trying to keep them safe.
teach.disconfirm: If people after frightening events showed no more scanning, startle or avoidance than anyone else, the account in this block would be wrong. Most people who have been through a serious frightening event recognise at least some of these changes in the weeks afterwards.

teach.h: Reminders can pull the past into the present.
teach.p:
For someone whose alarm is still tuned to a past danger, a reminder can bring that danger into the present with startling force. Reminders can be obvious, such as fireworks for a former soldier or a car horn for a crash survivor, or subtle: a smell, a tone of voice, a particular aftershave, being touched from behind, a crowded room, a raised voice, the time of year.

The response may look like any part of the defence cascade. A sudden freeze, the person going rigid and silent. A panic, with the breathing described in the chapter on breath. An angry outburst that seems to come from nowhere. Or a kind of absence, eyes glazed, the person not quite there, sometimes called dissociation. Afterwards the person may be exhausted, embarrassed or unaware of how long they were gone.

If you are with someone when this happens, the aim is to help them come back to the present. Speak calmly and use their name. Tell them where they are and that they are safe: *Sam. It's me. We're in the kitchen. It's Tuesday. You're safe.* Do not grab or touch them without asking; touch may feel like part of the threat. Give them space and a clear way out. Invite them to notice the room: the feel of the chair, their feet on the floor, something they can see.

Afterwards, do not demand an explanation. A simple *Are you all right? Do you want anything?* is enough. If they want to tell you what happened, listen.

When the past breaks into the present, your calm voice is a bridge back.
teach.disconfirm: If people having a reminder-triggered reaction were helped just as much by being touched or questioned as by calm words, space and grounding in the present, this block's advice would not matter. Survivors' accounts and clinical guidance consistently favour the calmer approach.

teach.p:
In 2014 the United States Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration set out six principles for what it called a trauma-informed approach: safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues. They were written for organisations, but they translate into everyday habits that make you safer company for anyone who has been through something frightening, whether or not you know about it.

Safety: notice how people arrange themselves, and let someone sit where they can see the door if they want to. Approach from the front, where you can be seen, rather than from behind. Trustworthiness and transparency: say what you are going to do before you do it. *I'm going to open the window.* *I'm just going to reach past you for the salt.* Do what you said you would do.

Choice and voice: offer choices wherever you can, and respect the answer. Ask before touching, always. Do not insist on hugs, closeness or particular seats. Collaboration: do things with people rather than to them. Peer support: some people find most help from others who have been through something similar, such as other veterans or other survivors. And cultural and historical awareness: some people carry trauma that belongs to their community's history as well as their own.

None of this requires you to know someone's history, and none of it costs you anything. It simply removes the small surprises, losses of control and uninvited touches that can set off an alarm that is still ringing.
teach.disconfirm: If explaining your actions, offering choices and asking before touch made no difference to how at ease people with a history of trauma felt with you, these habits would add nothing. Ask someone you know who has been through a frightening experience whether such things matter to them.

teach.h: Never make anyone tell their story.
teach.p:
When someone has been through something terrible, the instinct of many friends is to get them to talk about it, on the theory that talking will help it heal. Sometimes it does. But pressing someone to describe a traumatic event before they are ready can do harm.

For many years, emergency services and employers offered single-session psychological debriefing to people soon after a traumatic event, in which they were encouraged to go through what happened and their feelings about it. Reviews of the research found that it did not prevent later problems, and in some studies the people who had been debriefed did worse. Clinical guidelines now advise against routine debriefing of this kind. What helps in the early days is practical support, safety, rest and company, with talking available when the person chooses it.

The same applies in everyday life. Let the person decide whether, when and how much to tell you. If they do talk, listen without pressing for details, without questioning their account, and without asking why they did or did not do something. Believe them. Do not compare it with your own experiences, and do not tell their story to others.

If they choose not to talk, that is not a failure of trust. Your steady presence, practical help and patience may matter more than any conversation. Many survivors say that the people who helped most were the ones who simply stayed, and treated them normally.

Let them hold the story. Your job is to hold the space.
teach.disconfirm: If people pressed to describe traumatic events soon afterwards did better over time than people left to talk at their own pace, the advice in this block would be wrong. The reviews of early psychological debriefing found the opposite.

teach.p:
It is worth ending on the most hopeful fact in this chapter. Many people recover from frightening experiences on their own, with time, support and ordinary life. For those who do not, effective treatments exist. Clinical guidelines in many countries recommend trauma-focused psychological therapies, such as trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, for post-traumatic stress, and many people improve substantially with them, even years after the event.

So the most useful thing you can do, when someone's alarm has stayed on for more than about a month, when they are avoiding large parts of life, sleeping badly, drinking to cope, or struggling at work or at home, is to encourage them to see a doctor, and to make it practical. Many countries also have specialist services for veterans, for emergency workers and for survivors of assault, which people can often contact directly.

If the person talks about not wanting to go on, or you are worried for their safety, ask them directly whether they are thinking about suicide, and use the crisis resources in this app. Trauma raises that risk, and asking is safe.

And look after yourself. Hearing about traumatic events, or living alongside someone whose alarm is always on, takes a toll. It is ordinary to need support yourself, and getting it makes you a better support for them.

The body that learned to freeze can learn to feel safe again. Help makes it more likely.
teach.disconfirm: If people with persistent post-traumatic stress improved just as much without treatment as with trauma-focused therapy, encouraging professional help would add little. The evidence behind clinical guidelines suggests treatment helps many people substantially.

poseGallery.doCaption: 'Freezing is the body's response. It wasn't a choice.'
poseGallery.annotation: Tonic immobility is common and involuntary. Asking why someone did not fight adds blame to harm.

poseGallery.doCaption: Approaching where he can see you, and saying his name.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Coming up behind him and touching his shoulder.
poseGallery.annotation: After trauma, surprises and touch from behind can set off an alarm that is still ringing. Be seen, and be heard first.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting him choose whether, when and how much to say.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Pressing him to tell you everything that happened.
poseGallery.annotation: Pressing people to describe trauma early can do harm. Practical support and patience help more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seeing a body still trying to keep him safe, and staying.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading his jumpiness and short temper as weakness.
poseGallery.annotation: Hypervigilance, startle and irritability are the body's learned protection after a threat, not a flaw.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting near, letting her choose what to say
poseGallery.dontCaption: Pressing her for the details of what happened
poseGallery.annotation: Asking for details, or why she did not fight, adds blame. Belief, closeness without pressure and her choice about what to tell help more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Told, and believed, that freezing was not a choice
poseGallery.dontCaption: Alone with the shame of having frozen
poseGallery.annotation: Many survivors blame themselves for freezing. Hearing that it is what bodies do, from someone who believes them, can lift some of that weight.

caseStudy:
Chris, thirty-one, shares a flat with his friend Jamal, thirty-three. In October, Jamal is attacked and robbed on his way home from the station. He is bruised but not badly injured, and tells Chris he is fine. He goes back to work after a week.

Over the next month Chris notices changes. Jamal now walks home the long way, avoiding the high street. In the pub he takes the seat facing the door and keeps glancing at it. When a glass smashes behind the bar, he jumps so hard he spills his drink, then goes very quiet. He is short-tempered, which is not like him, and Chris hears him moving around the flat at three in the morning.

One evening Chris comes up behind Jamal in the kitchen and puts a hand on his shoulder to reach for a mug. Jamal goes rigid, then spins round with his fists up. He stares at Chris for a moment without seeming to see him. Chris steps back and says calmly, *Jamal. It's me. You're at home. You're safe.* After a few seconds Jamal lowers his hands, apologises, and sits down, shaking.

Chris does not ask what happened in October. He says he is sorry for startling him, and that from now on he will say something when he comes into a room. A few days later, on a walk, Jamal tells him a little about the attack: that he froze, could not shout, and has been furious with himself ever since. Chris tells him that freezing is one of the body's most common responses to danger, and not a choice.

In December, when the jumpiness and the broken sleep have not eased, Chris suggests he see his doctor and offers to go with him. Jamal is referred for trauma-focused therapy. By spring he is walking down the high street again, on good days.
observe: Notice how people arrange themselves in a room you enter: who sits facing the door, who takes the seat by the exit.
Notice your own habits of approach: whether you tend to come up behind people, touch without warning, or act without saying what you are about to do.
Notice how people around you react to a sudden loud noise, and how long it takes each of them to return to baseline.

drills.name: Announce Yourself
steps: For one day, say what you are about to do before you do it, whenever it involves someone else's space.
Approach people from where they can see you, rather than from behind.
Ask before any touch, however small.
Notice whether anyone responds differently from usual.
Write down which of these felt most unnatural to you, and why.
variations: Practise announcing yourself with a child, an older relative or a colleague, and notice whether they seem more at ease.
For one meeting or gathering, notice who sits facing the door, and make sure that seat is free for anyone who wants it.

drills.name: Grounding Script
steps: Write a short script for helping someone come back to the present: their name, who you are, where they are, the day, that they are safe.
Add two invitations to notice the room, such as their feet on the floor or something they can see.
Say the script aloud slowly until it feels natural.
Note what you would not do: grab, question, crowd.
Keep the script where you can find it.
variations: Adapt your script for a child, using simpler words and a familiar object they can hold or name.
Practise the script with a friend, taking turns to be the person who is frozen, and notice which phrases feel calming.

drills.name: Choice Audit
steps: Think of a setting you control, such as your home, your team meetings or a regular social event.
List the moments where people have no choice, such as where to sit, whether to speak or whether to be touched.
For each, write one way you could offer a choice.
Introduce one of these changes this week.
Note how people respond.
variations: Ask someone you trust which moments in your home or workplace feel least in their control, and add their answers to your list.
Choose one routine that always happens without warning, such as a fire drill or a loud announcement, and find a way to give notice.

drills.name: Words That Blame
steps: Write down any questions or phrases you might instinctively use with someone after a frightening event, such as why didn't you or you should have.
Mark each that implies they could or should have acted differently.
Write a replacement for each that conveys belief and support.
Write one true sentence you could say to someone who blames themselves for freezing.
Practise saying it aloud.
variations: Write the replacement sentences on a card and keep it in your wallet or phone, so that they are there when shock takes your words.
Practise saying "I believe you" aloud until it feels natural, since it is often the hardest and most important sentence.

drills.name: Know the Routes
steps: Find out how someone where you live can be referred for trauma-focused therapy, through a doctor or directly.
Find any specialist services for veterans, emergency workers or survivors of assault in your area.
Find the crisis resources in this app for your region.
Write two practical offers you could make to someone who needs help.
Keep these notes where you can find them quickly.
variations: Find out whether your workplace has a trauma support service or employee assistance line, and how to refer yourself or a colleague.
Write down how you would explain, in one sentence, that trauma treatment works even years after an event.

quiz.q: During a frightening assault, a man froze and could not fight back or shout. What does the research on freezing suggest?
options: That he was too weak or too frightened to protect himself properly
That he must, at some level, have been willing to go along with it
That freezing is an involuntary defence; it says nothing of consent or courage
That he was in shock and will not remember anything about what happened
quiz.explain: Tonic immobility is a last-resort defence driven by ancient brain systems, not a decision. It is common, and survivors often blame themselves for it, which adds to their distress. It tells you nothing about consent or courage.

quiz.q: In Möller and colleagues' study of women seen at a clinic after sexual assault, roughly how many reported significant tonic immobility?
options: About seven in ten
About one in ten
Almost none of them
Only those who were injured
quiz.explain: Around seventy percent reported significant immobility and nearly half extreme immobility, and those who froze were more likely to develop post-traumatic stress and severe depression. Freezing is common, not rare.

quiz.q: In the defence cascade described by Kozlowska and colleagues, what is tonic immobility?
options: A deliberate decision to stay still so as not to be noticed by an attacker
A form of fainting caused by low blood sugar during a stressful situation
A trained response that soldiers and police learn in order to stay calm
An involuntary, last-resort immobility when escape seems impossible
quiz.explain: It comes after arousal, fight or flight and alert freezing, when the threat seems overwhelming. The person cannot move or cry out, often while fully aware, and does not choose it.

quiz.q: Since being mugged, your friend jumps at sudden noises and sits with his back to the wall. You need to wake him from a nap on the sofa. What fits?
options: Shake his shoulder firmly so that he wakes up quickly and fully
Call his name from the doorway, where he can see you, before you approach
Creep in quietly so as not to startle him, then tap him gently
Let him sleep on, since waking him is likely to upset him whatever you do
quiz.explain: After a threat, surprise and touch can set off an alarm that is still on. Being seen and heard first, from a little distance, lets him wake into safety rather than into a reminder.

quiz.q: Which of these fits a trauma-informed approach in everyday life?
options: Insisting on a hug to show you care, even if they hesitate at first
Encouraging them to describe what happened in detail straight away
Saying what you will do before you do it, and offering choices
Treating them as fragile, and making all of their decisions for them
quiz.explain: Transparency and choice restore some of the control that trauma takes away. Insisting on touch, pressing for the story and taking over decisions all remove control again.

quiz.q: Two months after a serious car crash, a colleague still has nightmares, avoids driving and is constantly on edge. What fits this chapter?
options: Encourage him to see a doctor, since trauma-focused therapies help many
Tell him it has been long enough and that he needs to get back behind the wheel
Ask him to tell you exactly what happened, since talking about it will help
Leave it, since these things always settle down on their own in the end
quiz.explain: Signs that persist beyond a month and disrupt life are a reason to seek help, and effective treatments exist. Pushing him to drive or to tell the story can make things worse; making a doctor's appointment practical helps.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of SAMHSA's six principles for a trauma-informed approach?
options: Empowerment, voice and choice for the people involved
Speed, firmness and control over every decision
Debriefing everyone in detail as soon as possible
Strict silence about the past, to avoid upsetting anyone
quiz.explain: SAMHSA's six principles are safety; trustworthiness and transparency; peer support; collaboration and mutuality; empowerment, voice and choice; and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues. Offering choice is one of the simplest ways to apply them.

quiz.q: Whenever voices rise in an argument, your partner goes completely still, stares at the floor, wraps her arms round herself and stops answering. What fits this chapter best?
options: Raise your voice further, since she is clearly refusing to engage with you
Lower your voice, stop asking questions and agree to come back to it later
Tell her that silence is a form of punishment and that it has to stop
Keep asking her what is wrong until she finally tells you what she thinks
quiz.explain: Her stillness fits a freeze, which raised voices can trigger in people who grew up with frightening adults. Pressing pushes her further into it; lowering your voice and pausing lets her come back.

quiz.q: Someone says that the best way to help people after a traumatic event is to have them go through every detail of it in one session straight away. What does the research suggest?
options: It is right, since talking it all through at once always prevents later problems
Single-session debriefing did not prevent later problems and may have harmed some
It is right, but only if the session lasts at least three hours without a break
It is wrong, since people should never talk about traumatic events at all
quiz.explain: Reviews found that single-session debriefing soon after a trauma did not prevent post-traumatic stress and might have made some people worse. Let people choose whether and when to talk, and offer professional help if they are struggling.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you know who has been through a frightening experience: an accident, an assault, combat, a disaster, a violent home. What, if anything, changed in how they carried their body afterwards: how they sat, how they reacted to noise, where they would and would not go? How did people around them read those changes? Then think about your own habits: which of the trauma-informed habits in this chapter would make you safer company for them, and which will you practise this week?
reflection.guidance: You do not need to know the details of what happened to answer this, and you should not seek them out. Focus on what was visible and on how it was read. Many people realise that someone they thought of as jumpy or short-tempered was carrying something heavy. The habit you choose should be concrete: announcing yourself, asking before touch, offering a choice.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read freezing as consent, weakness or willingness, and to ask a survivor why they did not fight. The second is to misread the after-effects of trauma, treating hypervigilance as paranoia, startle as nervousness and irritability as bad temper. The third is to set off the alarm by accident: coming up from behind, touching without asking, making sudden moves, surprising someone who cannot bear surprise. The fourth is to press for the story, believing that talking always heals, when pressing early can harm. And the fifth is to leave it too long, waiting for signs that have lasted months to settle on their own. Be predictable, offer choice, ask before touch, believe people, and help them reach treatment that works.

moreCases.title: The firefighter at the barbecue
moreCases.scene:
Gareth, forty-six, retired from the fire service two years ago after twenty years on the job. At a friend's summer barbecue, someone lets
  the coals flare and a pile of burgers catches, sending up a cloud of black smoke. Most of the guests laugh and cheer. Gareth, standing nearby
  with a drink, goes rigid. His face drains of colour, his eyes fix on the smoke and he stops breathing for several seconds. Then he puts his
  drink down on the wall, very carefully, and walks quickly round the side of the house.

  One of the guests, who knows Gareth slightly, calls after him, "Not keen on a bit of smoke, for a fireman!" A couple of people laugh. Gareth's
  wife, Helen, goes after him and finds him sitting on the front step, pale and shaking, staring at the pavement.

  When the host, Paul, comes round to see what happened, Helen tells him quietly that there was a house fire, years ago, in which Gareth could not
  reach a child. He does not talk about it.

Gareth has never told anyone outside his family about the fire, and he has never seen anyone about it. His old station had a counselling service, but going to it, he once said to Helen, would have been "the end of the banter for ever".

Helen has seen this before: at a garage fire on the news, at a smoky pub, once at a bonfire. Each time, Gareth goes still, then leaves, then says nothing about it afterwards. She has learned to follow him without fuss.
moreCases.misread:
The guest read Gareth's reaction as an odd weakness in a firefighter, something to tease. The others read it as an overreaction to a bit of barbecue smoke. None of them knew that the smoke had pulled a past danger into the present.

And the joke turned a moment of private terror into a public embarrassment, which is often what makes people who have been through trauma hide their reactions even more carefully next time.

The guest's joke also rested on a common belief: that people who face danger for a living should be immune to it. Often the opposite is true. They have simply seen more of it.
moreCases.betterRead:
A reminder, here the sight and smell of thick smoke, can trigger the body's defence cascade as though the original danger were happening again. Gareth's stillness, held breath, fixed gaze and then rapid exit fit a freeze followed by flight, not a man being squeamish. Emergency workers and soldiers often carry reactions like this for years, frequently in silence, because their training and their workplaces have taught them that reactions are weakness. Paul's better response was simple. He did not ask what had happened in the fire. He sat down on the step beside Gareth, said he was sorry about the joke, and asked if Gareth would like to stay out front for a while, with a drink brought out to him. Later he took the guest aside and asked him, without explanation, to lay off. A few weeks afterwards, Helen mentioned that Gareth had started seeing someone through a service for former emergency workers.

Paul also made sure, at his next barbecue, that the grill was set up at the far end of the garden, and said nothing about why.

moreCases.title: The friend who asked the wrong question
moreCases.scene:
Laura, twenty-nine, and her friend Beth have known each other since school. One evening, after a few weeks of Beth seeming distant and
  cancelling plans, Beth tells Laura that she was sexually assaulted by a man she met at a work event. She tells it haltingly, looking at her
  hands, and says very little about what happened. She says she could not move, could not shout, could not do anything. She says it over and
  over: she just froze.

  Laura is horrified and angry on her friend's behalf. Without thinking, she asks, "But why didn't you scream? Couldn't you have pushed him
  off?"

  Beth goes silent. She pulls her knees up to her chest, wraps her arms round them and looks at the floor. After a minute she says she should
  probably go home.

Beth has not told anyone else, not her parents, not her flatmate, not her manager at work, where the man is a contractor she still sometimes sees in the lift. She says she has not slept properly since.

Laura has also noticed changes in Beth over the past month that she had not understood. Beth has stopped going to the gym, where she used to go every morning. She jumps when her phone rings. When they went for a drink a fortnight ago, Beth insisted on sitting in a corner, facing the room, and left early when a group of men came in, saying she had a headache.
moreCases.misread:
Laura's question came from shock and from a common belief that a person who is attacked will fight or shout, and that not doing so needs explaining. Beth heard it as what she already feared: that she was to blame for not resisting.

Her question also shifted the focus from what the man had done to what Beth had not, which is a shift survivors hear constantly and which keeps many of them silent.

She also, without meaning to, treated Beth's freezing as the part of the story that needed explaining, rather than what the man had done.
moreCases.betterRead: Freezing is one of the body's most common responses to inescapable danger, and it is not chosen. In Möller and colleagues' study of women seen after a sexual assault, around seven in ten reported significant immobility during it, despite wanting to resist. Survivors who froze often blame themselves, and a question about why they did not fight confirms that blame. Laura realised what she had done as soon as Beth curled up. She said, "I'm so sorry, that was a terrible thing to ask. Freezing is what bodies do. It wasn't your fault, and I believe you." She did not ask for details. She asked whether Beth wanted to stay, and whether there was anything she could do. Beth stayed. Later that week, Laura found the details of a specialist sexual violence support service and gave them to Beth, saying she would go with her if she wanted. Beth went, alone, a month later, and told Laura afterwards that the counsellor had said the same thing about freezing, and that hearing it twice had helped.

moreCases.title: The warehouse worker who did not answer
moreCases.scene:
Amir, thirty, came to Britain as a refugee from Syria four years ago and now works in a distribution warehouse. He is quiet, careful and
  reliable. His new shift supervisor, Wayne, has started to find him frustrating. Twice, when a pallet has crashed to the floor nearby, Amir has
  stopped dead in the middle of the aisle, rigid, staring at nothing, and has not responded when Wayne shouted his name. Once he dropped what he was
  holding and crouched behind a shelving unit. Afterwards he says sorry and goes back to work without explanation.

  Wayne thinks Amir is not paying attention, or is deliberately ignoring him. He has started shouting louder, and coming up behind Amir to tap him
  on the shoulder when he wants something, which makes Amir jump violently.

  A colleague who has worked with Amir for two years, Kasia, tells Wayne that he has got it wrong.

Amir has never talked about the war at work. Kasia knows only that he lost his brother, because he mentioned it once, briefly, when she asked about his family, and then changed the subject.

Kasia has noticed something else. On days when there has been a crash, Amir eats lunch alone in his car rather than in the canteen, and comes back quieter. He has never taken a day off sick in two years, and he is the first to volunteer for extra shifts.
moreCases.misread:
Wayne read Amir's stillness and failure to answer as inattention or defiance, and responded with the things most likely to set off the alarm again: louder shouting and touches from behind.

He also took the crouching as theatrical, when it was the most protective thing Amir's body knew to do in the presence of a sudden crash.

He also took Amir's silence afterwards as sullenness. A man who has just come back from a freeze often has no words for it, and no wish to explain it to a supervisor he barely knows. Asking him to explain would have been one more demand.
moreCases.betterRead:
Sudden loud noises, such as a crash, a bang or a shout, are among the commonest reminders for people who have lived through violence or war. Amir's freeze, his fixed stare, his failure to hear his name and his crouch behind the shelving fit a body responding to danger, not a man ignoring his supervisor. Shouting louder and tapping him from behind made each episode worse. Kasia suggested what trauma-informed habits describe: approach from the front, where he can see you; say his name at an ordinary volume; tell him what you want before you touch anything; and, after a freeze, give him a moment and speak slowly. Wayne, a little embarrassed, tried it. He also asked Amir, privately and without asking about the past, whether there was anything at work that would help. Amir asked whether he could work in the aisles furthest from the loading bay, where the crashes were rarer. Wayne moved him, and the freezes became much less frequent.

Wayne also stopped the habit of tapping people from behind with everyone on the shift, and found that several other workers were relieved.

moreCases.title: The girlfriend who went still
moreCases.scene:
Tom and Lily have been together for a year. They rarely argue, but when they do, a pattern has started to frustrate Tom. As his voice
  rises, Lily stops talking. She goes very still, her face blank, her eyes fixed on a point on the floor, her arms wrapped around herself. She
  does not answer his questions. Sometimes she seems not to hear him at all. Tom finds this maddening. He reads it as stonewalling, a refusal to
  engage, and it makes him louder.

  After one argument, he tells a friend that Lily "just shuts down and ignores me, like I'm not even there". His friend suggests he asks her
  about it, at a calm moment, rather than in the middle of a row.

  When Tom does, a few days later, Lily tells him that she grew up in a house where her father shouted a great deal, and where silence and
  stillness were the safest things to do. She says that when a man's voice gets loud, she goes somewhere else, and cannot get back until it is
  quiet.

Tom has also noticed that, after an argument, Lily is exhausted for hours, and sometimes has a headache the next day. He had put this down to her sulking.

Tom has also noticed that Lily cannot watch films with shouting in them, and that she goes quiet when his friends get loud and boisterous at the pub. He had thought she just did not like them.
moreCases.misread:
Tom read Lily's stillness as a deliberate withdrawal, a form of punishment or contempt, because that is what silence in an argument often means. He did not see that her body was doing what it had learned to do to survive.

And Tom's louder voice, meant to reach her, was the very thing that kept her away. The harder he pressed, the further she went.

He also took her exhaustion afterwards as sulking, when a freeze can leave the body drained for hours.
moreCases.betterRead:
Freezing is not only a response to extreme events. For people who grew up with frightening adults, ordinary raised voices can set off the same defence cascade years later. Lily's fixed gaze, her arms wrapped around herself, her silence and her apparent deafness fit a freeze, and pressing her at that moment, with a louder voice, pushes her further into it. Tom's better approach was the opposite of his instinct. They agreed that if Lily went still, he would lower his voice, stop asking questions, and say something like, "I'm not angry with you. Let's stop for a bit." He would sit down rather than stand over her. They would come back to the subject later, when she was ready. It felt strange to Tom at first to stop an argument he had not finished. He found that the arguments they came back to were shorter and kinder than the ones he had pressed on with.

Lily also found it easier, over time, to say "I'm going still" before it took hold completely, which gave them both a few seconds' warning.

workedReading.title: Bonfire night
workedReading.scene:
Kemi has taken her children to a community bonfire and fireworks display in the local park. As the first rockets go up with a series of loud bangs, she notices a man standing a few metres away, alone, in his fifties. He has gone completely rigid. His face is pale, his eyes are wide and fixed on the sky, his hands are clenched at his sides and he does not seem to be breathing. When the next bang comes, he flinches hard and half crouches. People around him are cheering. Nobody else seems to have noticed.

Kemi is not trained in anything beyond basic first aid, and she hesitates. She is aware that approaching a stranger could frighten him more, and that walking away would leave him alone.

She also notices that she does not know whether he is with anyone. He seems to be alone, and the people around him are watching the sky, not him.

steps.label: Notice the freeze
steps.text:
Kemi notes the cluster: sudden rigidity, pallor, a fixed stare, clenched hands, held breath, a flinch and a half crouch at each bang. In a crowd that is cheering, this is not excitement or cold. It fits a body responding to danger. She also notes that she does not know why, and that she does not need to.

She also notices that she is calm herself, which matters. If she were frightened, she would be likely to rush, and rushing towards someone in a freeze can make it worse.

She also notes that the reaction repeats at each bang, which tells her it is tied to the noise rather than to something else in the crowd, such as a person he is frightened of.

steps.label: Check for an emergency
steps.text:
She considers whether he might be unwell in another way: a heart problem, a fall about to happen. His colour is pale but he is upright, and the timing of his reactions matches the bangs. She decides to approach, and to call for the first-aid volunteers if he seems physically unwell or does not respond at all.

She also keeps half an eye on the first-aid tent, so that she knows where help is if she needs it quickly.

She also reminds herself that she can be wrong about the cause and still help. Whatever is happening, a calm person, a choice and a quieter place will not make it worse.

steps.label: Approach where he can see you
steps.text:
She leaves her children with her sister and walks round so that she is in front of him, at an angle, where he can see her coming, rather than approaching from behind. She stops a little more than an arm's length away. She does not touch him. She says, at an ordinary volume, "Hello, I'm Kemi. Are you all right?"

She also keeps her hands visible and her movements slow. A sudden gesture, even a friendly one, could look like the very threat his body is braced for.

She also chooses not to say "Don't worry" or "It's only fireworks". Both would tell him that his body is wrong, which it is not; it is doing what it learned to do.

steps.label: Offer choice and a way out
steps.text:
He looks at her as if from a long way off and nods slightly, but does not speak. She says, "The fireworks are loud. Would you like to walk over to the car park with me, where it's quieter?" The question gives him a choice and an exit. He nods again, and they walk slowly to the edge of the park, with her beside him rather than in front.

She also walks at his pace, which is slow and stiff, and does not try to hurry him or guide him by the arm. He finds his own way, a step behind her shoulder.

She also makes sure the route to the car park is clear and does not lead them through the thickest part of the crowd, where being jostled from behind might set off his alarm again.

steps.label: Help him come back
steps.text:
At the car park, where the bangs are muffled, Kemi speaks slowly and calmly. She tells him where they are and that he is safe. She asks him to notice his feet on the ground and to tell her what colour her coat is. She breathes slowly herself. Over a few minutes his breathing returns, his hands open and he says, hoarsely, that he is sorry, he does not know what came over him.

She keeps her questions simple and concrete. A man coming back from a freeze can answer what colour a coat is far more easily than how he is feeling.

She also keeps her own breathing slow and audible, without commenting on it. People coming back from a freeze often fall into step with a calm person nearby, as the chapter on breath described.

steps.label: Do not ask for the story
steps.text:
Kemi does not ask what happened to him or why fireworks affect him. She says there is nothing to be sorry for, that loud bangs are hard for lots of people, and asks whether there is anyone she can call. He says his name is Ian and that his wife is at home, a few streets away. He says he thought he would be all right this year.

She also resists the urge to tell him that she understands. She does not, and he would know it.

She also offers practical help: a bottle of water from her bag, and to wait with him until his wife arrives. Practical help asks nothing of him except yes or no.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Ian rings his wife, who comes to collect him. Before she leaves, she thanks Kemi and says quietly that Ian served in the army, and that bonfire night is always hard. Kemi returns to her children. She notes that she never learned what had happened to him, and that she did not need to. What helped was approaching where he could see her, giving him a choice and a way out, staying calm and slow, and leaving the story to him.

She also mentions to the organisers, afterwards, that a quiet area away from the fireworks might help some people next year. They put up a sign for one the following November.

She also thinks, on the way home, about how close she came to not approaching him at all. Most people in the crowd would have helped if they had noticed. The difference was only that she was looking.

moreFailures.title: Asking why they did not fight or run
moreFailures.body:
"Why didn't you scream?" "Why didn't you just leave?" "Couldn't you have fought him off?" These questions are often asked out of shock, love or anger on the survivor's behalf, and they are among the most damaging things a survivor can hear. They assume that resistance was possible and that not resisting needs explaining. The research on the defence cascade and on tonic immobility shows that freezing is common, automatic and not chosen. Many survivors already blame themselves for it, and questions like these confirm the blame. Instead say what is true: freezing is what bodies do in danger, it was not your fault, and I believe you.

It also helps to remember that the same applies to men. Men who have been assaulted often face even more disbelief about freezing, because of beliefs that men should always be able to fight back. Freezing is just as automatic in men.

It also helps to know that survivors are often asked these questions by the people closest to them, sometimes repeatedly. If you have asked one, it is never too late to say that you understand now, and that you are sorry.

Questions about what the survivor was wearing, drinking or doing beforehand carry the same blame, and do the same harm. None of them is a friend's business unless the survivor chooses to raise it.

moreFailures.title: Reading the alarm as character
moreFailures.body:
After trauma, the body can stay on alert for months or years: jumping at noises, scanning rooms, sitting with the back to a wall, snapping at small irritations, avoiding certain places. Each of these is easy to read as a flaw: paranoia, nervousness, bad temper, rudeness, laziness. These readings make the person's life harder, because they add judgment to a body that is already working overtime to keep them safe. Before deciding that someone is jumpy, cold or difficult, consider that their alarm may still be tuned to a danger you know nothing about, and make it a little easier for them, rather than harder.

It also helps to notice the strengths that come with the alarm. Many people who have been through danger are extremely good in a crisis, alert, steady and quick to act. The same body that jumps at a slammed door may be the one you want beside you in an emergency.

It also helps to make small allowances without asking for explanations: letting someone choose their seat, warning them before a loud noise, not taking it personally when they leave a crowded room.

Irritability deserves particular patience. A body that is constantly on alert has little left over for frustration, and a person who snaps at small things may be exhausted by vigilance rather than short-tempered by nature.

moreFailures.title: Setting off the alarm for fun
moreFailures.body:
Some workplaces and friendship groups have a culture of pranks and surprises: jumping out from behind doors, banging things to make people jump, coming up from behind with a loud noise, play-fighting without warning. For most people these are harmless. For someone whose alarm is still tuned to danger, they can trigger a full freeze or panic, and the laughter that follows adds shame. You rarely know who has been through what. A culture of announcing yourself, approaching from the front and asking before touching costs nothing and makes a room safer for everyone in it.

If someone does react badly to a surprise, the kindest response is a quiet apology and nothing more. Asking them why they reacted so strongly, or telling them it was only a joke, makes it worse.

Workplaces that use loud alarms, sudden announcements or drills can help by giving notice where possible. A message saying "there will be a fire alarm test at eleven" costs nothing and spares some people a great deal.

Children are especially affected by surprises and play-fighting if they have been through something frightening. A child who screams or freezes when an adult jumps out at them is not being silly, and should not be laughed at.

moreFailures.title: Playing therapist
moreFailures.body:
When someone has been through something terrible, a caring friend may want to help them process it: asking them to go through what happened, encouraging them to feel their feelings, interpreting their reactions, or announcing that they must have PTSD. Reviews of single-session debriefing found that pressing people to go through traumatic events soon afterwards did not prevent later problems and might have made some worse. A friend's job is different from a therapist's. It is to be safe, steady company; to believe them; to let them choose whether, when and how much to tell; to notice if they seem stuck; and to help them reach professional help if they want it.

It also helps to look after yourself. Hearing about someone's trauma can be distressing, and friends sometimes carry more than they realise. Talking to someone you trust, without sharing identifying details, can help you stay steady for them.

It also helps to resist labels. Telling someone they have PTSD, or that they are traumatised, can frighten them, or make them feel broken. Describing what you have noticed, and asking how they are, leaves them free to find their own words.

questions.q: Is freezing a sign of weakness?
questions.a:
No. Freezing is part of the body's automatic defence cascade, which Kozlowska and colleagues describe across animals and humans. When escape or fighting seems impossible, many bodies stop moving, sometimes in a state of alert stillness and sometimes in tonic immobility, when the person cannot move or speak even if they want to. It is not chosen, and it is extremely common: in Möller and colleagues' study, around seven in ten women seen after a sexual assault reported significant immobility. Freezing says nothing about a person's courage or character. It says that their body was trying to survive.

It also helps to say this to anyone who blames themselves for freezing, including yourself. Many people carry that shame for years, and hearing that freezing is common and automatic can be the start of putting it down.

It may also help to know that animals freeze in the same way, and that the response is ancient. A rabbit that goes still in the headlights is not choosing to; neither is a person.

questions.q: What is the difference between freezing and tonic immobility?
questions.a:
In the defence cascade Kozlowska and colleagues describe, freezing is a state of alert stillness: the body is primed to move but holds still, often while it assesses the threat, and the person may be able to act if a way out appears. Tonic immobility comes later, when escape seems impossible: the body becomes still and unresponsive, and the person may be unable to move or call out at all, even though they are aware. Both are automatic. In everyday conversation, people often use "freeze" for both, which is fine, as long as nobody assumes that someone who froze could have chosen to move.

It also helps to know that people often cannot remember clearly what happened during tonic immobility, or remember it in fragments. That is not a sign that they are confused or making things up. Memory under extreme threat often works differently.

Some survivors also describe a sense of watching from outside their body, or of time slowing down. These experiences are common during extreme threat, and they are part of the same protective cascade.

questions.q: Should I encourage someone to talk about what happened?
questions.a:
Let them lead. Some people want to talk about a frightening experience soon afterwards, and some do not, and both are normal. Pressing someone to describe a traumatic event before they are ready can do harm, as the research on single-session debriefing found. What helps is making it clear that you are there if they want to talk, believing what they tell you, listening without interrupting or interrogating, and not asking for details they have not offered. If they never want to tell you, that is their choice. Many people find it easier to talk to a trained professional than to a friend, and that is fine too.

If someone does want to talk, it helps to let them stop whenever they like, without asking them to finish. A story told in pieces, over months, is still being told.

It also helps to know what not to do if they do talk: do not ask for more detail than they offer, do not ask why, do not tell them how they should feel, and do not tell anyone else without their permission.

If you are the person who went through it, the same applies: you do not owe anyone your story. You can choose whom to tell, how much, and when, and you can change your mind.

questions.q: How can I tell whether someone has PTSD?
questions.a:
You cannot, and you should not try. Post-traumatic stress disorder is a diagnosis made by a professional, and the signs a friend might notice, such as jumpiness, nightmares, avoidance, irritability and sleeping badly, are common in the weeks after any frightening event and often settle by themselves. What you can notice is whether they are settling. If, more than a month or so after the event, someone is still struggling with these things, or they are getting in the way of work, relationships or sleep, it is worth suggesting, gently, that they talk to their doctor. Effective treatments exist, and they work even years after the event.

If you are worried about their safety, for example if they talk about not wanting to be here, 2.13 describes what to do, and that takes priority over waiting to see whether things settle.

It can also help to know that the early weeks after a frightening event are often the hardest, and that many reactions in this period are a normal part of recovery rather than signs that something has gone wrong.

For children, the signs may look different: clinginess, bed-wetting, play that repeats the frightening event, or new fears. A child's doctor or school can advise if these last.

questions.q: What should I do if someone freezes or panics in front of me?
questions.a:
Stay calm and slow. Approach where they can see you, and do not grab or touch them without asking. Say your name and theirs if you know it, at an ordinary volume. Tell them where they are and that they are safe. Offer a choice, such as moving somewhere quieter. Invite them to notice the present: their feet on the floor, something they can see, the sound of your voice. Breathe slowly yourself. Do not ask what is wrong or what happened. Wait. When they come back, let them lead. If they seem physically unwell, or do not come back, call for medical help.

Afterwards, it often helps to check in a day or two later, briefly, without asking about the episode itself: "Just wanted to see how you're doing."

If you are with a child who freezes or panics, the same principles apply, with even more emphasis on calm, slow speech, getting down to their level and staying with them until they feel safe again.

questions.q: Does trauma always cause lasting harm?
questions.a:
No. Most people who go through a frightening event are shaken for a while and then recover, with time, support and ordinary life. Some find that the experience changes them in ways they value. A minority develop lasting problems such as post-traumatic stress, and for them effective treatments exist: clinical guidelines recommend trauma-focused therapies such as trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy and EMDR, and many people improve substantially with them. The most useful message a friend can give is that recovery is possible, that help works, and that asking for it is a strong thing to do.

It also helps to know that support for people who have been through particular kinds of trauma, such as veterans, emergency workers, refugees and survivors of sexual violence, is often available from specialist services as well as from doctors.

It may also help to know that recovery is not always a straight line. People who are doing well may have a bad week around an anniversary or after a reminder, and that does not mean they have gone backwards.

And if you went through something frightening years ago and are still affected, it is not too late. Many people start treatment decades later and still benefit.

watch.title: How the body keeps the score on trauma
watch.notice: The psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk on how trauma is held in the body. Listen for what he says about freezing and shutting down, and why they are protective responses rather than weakness.
